blocks.text: The Evergreen Auto-Renewal Trap and Cure-Period Timing Errors

When evaluating billing traps mistakes how to fire and transition cleaning vendors, the single largest financial penalty stems from misreading the interplay between the contract anniversary date, the notice window, and the mandatory cure window. Many national and regional janitorial contracts include an evergreen rollover provision: unless the client delivers written notice via certified mail 60 days prior to the annual anniversary date, the agreement automatically renews for another 12-month term.

Even when a contract permits termination for cause at any time, a hidden procedural trap catches facility managers off guard. If your agreement requires a 15-day written Notice to Cure followed by a 30-day termination notice if deficiencies persist, you are actually looking at a 45-day minimum exit timeline. If an office manager signs a binding start date with a new contractor for the 1st of next month while still inside the incumbent's cure window, the outgoing contractor only has to send a supervisor out for two nights to claim the breach was 'cured'—legally obligating you to pay both vendors for the overlap period.

blocks.title: Beware of 'Cure Reset' Language in Multi-Tenant and Corporate MSAs
blocks.text: Watch out for contract language stating that any single corrected inspection resets the default counter to zero. When drafting your replacement agreement, demand a 'Three-Strike Chronic Default' clause: if the vendor receives three written deficiency notices within any rolling 90-day period, the client may terminate upon 15 days notice without granting a fourth cure window.
Amortized Floor Care Clawbacks and Unbilled Visit Proration Loopholes

A second high-dollar pitfall hides inside bundled monthly janitorial retainers that include quarterly or semi-annual specialty floor maintenance. Many commercial offices bundle quarterly carpet hot-water extraction or VCT machine scrub-and-recoat services into their monthly base invoice at an amortized rate of $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month. In a 15,000 sq ft office, that equals $450 to $900 per month set aside for periodic floor work.
The billing loophole operates in two directions depending on when you terminate:

items: The Unperformed Escrow Loss: You pay the $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft monthly floor-care amortization for five straight months, but the vendor delays scheduling the quarterly carpet extraction or VCT waxing. When you terminate in month five, the vendor keeps the accumulated $2,250 to $4,500 in collected floor-care fees without ever bringing an extractor or burnisher on site.

The Front-Loaded Clawback Invoice: Conversely, if a new vendor performs an initial VCT strip-and-wax or deep carpet extraction in month one and amortizes the cost over a 12-month contract, terminating them in month four triggers an immediate lump-sum 'unamortized specialty labor' invoice billed at specialty rates of $55 to $95 per hour.

The 4.33-Week Mid-Month Proration Distortion: Flat monthly contracts assume 4.33 weeks per month (21.65 visits per month for a 5x-week daily schedule, or 13.0 visits for a 3x-week schedule). When terminating mid-month, vendors frequently divide the monthly retainer by 20 workdays instead of actual scheduled visits, overcharging by 8% to 12% on the final partial invoice.

blocks.text: The Final-Month Consumables Dump and Restocking Surcharge

When your janitorial vendor supplies paper towels, facial tissue, hand soap, and trash can liners on a cost-plus pass-through basis—rather than a fixed per-square-foot consumables rate of $0.012 to $0.025 per sq ft per visit—watch out for the 'final-month inventory dump.' Once a route supervisor learns an account is cancelling, some vendors deliver a 60-to-90-day supply of marked-up paper cases and liner boxes during week two of the notice period, billing them immediately to your final invoice. Worse, on the final night of service, poorly supervised crews occasionally walk out with unopened cases from the janitor closet that your company already paid for.

To stop consumables markups and transition leakage permanently, unbundle commodity liners and office tissue from the janitorial labor contract and stock them under your own facility purchasing account. For workstation wastebaskets, stocking the Boardwalk 24x33 Low-Cost Office Deskside Trash Can Liners (1000-Case)—an 8-micron high-density liner in coreless rolls sized for 12-to-16-quart desk bins—gives your facility months of controlled inventory in a single master carton. For breakrooms and copy rooms where sharp packaging punishes thin bags, the Genuine Joe 33x39 Heavy-Duty 33-Gallon Can Liners (100-Case) provide 1.5-mil puncture-resistant flat-pack protection. Similarly, keeping a facility-owned case of Kleenex Professional Facial Tissue Cube Boxes for Offices (36-Case, featuring 2-ply FSC-certified 95-sheet cube boxes) for conference rooms and reception desks prevents outgoing vendors from padding their final invoice with overpriced boutique tissue charges.
Non-Solicitation Clauses and Hiring Incumbent Day Porters

Often, an office manager wants to fire a disorganized janitorial company—because corporate billing is unresponsive or night supervision is nonexistent—while keeping a trusted daytime porter or lead evening cleaner who knows the building intimately. Before you ask the incoming janitorial contractor to hire that worker, read the 'Non-Solicitation of Employees' paragraph in your outgoing MSA.

Most commercial cleaning agreements prohibit the client (or any replacement contractor hired by the client) from employing the vendor's assigned personnel during the contract term and for 6 to 12 months post-termination. Violating this clause typically triggers a liquidated placement fee equal to 25% to 50% of the worker's annual wages, or roughly $8,000 to $18,000 per employee. If retaining a specific day porter is essential to your facility operations, negotiate a written waiver from the outgoing vendor as part of your final invoice settlement before the incoming vendor puts that technician on payroll.

faqs.q: Can an outgoing cleaning vendor charge us for unamortized floor waxing if they never gave us a separate floor schedule?
faqs.a: Only if your executed contract explicitly states that initial startup floor work (such as VCT strip-and-wax or carpet hot-water extraction) was discounted contingent upon completing a full 12-month term. If the contract simply lists a flat monthly price with quarterly floor care included at $0.03 to $0.06 per sq ft per month, the vendor cannot invent a retroactive hourly charge ($55 to $95/hr) upon a valid termination.

faqs.q: What happens if the outgoing vendor stops emptying trash or cleaning restrooms during the 30-day notice period?
faqs.a: Document every missed task with timestamped photographs on the morning following the shift and email a formal deduction notice to the vendor's corporate address. Under standard commercial contract remedies, if a vendor abandons service during the notice period, you can deduct the pro-rata per-visit cost (monthly rate divided by 4.33 weeks times weekly frequency) and apply those funds toward emergency coverage.

faqs.q: How do we stop an automatic 12-month evergreen renewal if we missed the 60-day notice window by two weeks?
faqs.a: Immediately shift from a 'termination for convenience' track to a 'termination for cause' audit. Review your contract's scope of work line by line—including OSHA SDS binder availability, HEPA vacuum filtration requirements, restroom disinfection dwell times, and verified labor hours. If the vendor is out of compliance, issue a formal Notice to Cure; evergreen renewal clauses do not protect a vendor who fails to cure a material breach of scope.

faqs.q: Should we bundle or unbundle trash liners and paper consumables when signing the replacement vendor?
faqs.a: For offices under 25,000 sq ft, purchasing your own high-density deskside liners, 1.5-mil 33-gallon breakroom liners, and paper products directly—and storing them in a locked facility supply cabinet—eliminates 25% to 40% vendor distributor markups and prevents inventory disputes if you ever switch cleaning vendors again.
